Note::hex_encode¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::hex_encode() const

Encode Every Cell As Hexadecimal¶

hex_encode() replaces each cell with the lowercase hexadecimal representation of its bytes: every input byte becomes exactly two hex digits, with no separators and no 0x prefix. Use it when you need a fully unambiguous, fixed-ratio ASCII rendering of arbitrary bytes — a hash-like identifier, a debug dump, a value for a system that rejects Base64’s +//.

Compared with base64_encode, hex is simpler to read and byte-aligned (2 characters per byte, always), at the cost of being twice the size rather than four-thirds. Like Base64 it operates on the bytes of the cell, so "café" encodes its five UTF-8 bytes.

The result is a UTF-8-mode Note (hex digits are ASCII). The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note; an empty cell encodes to an empty cell. hex_decode is the exact inverse.

Example 1: A Batch¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"Hi!", "café", ""}).hex_encode())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, encoding=utf8)
["486921", "636166c3a9", ""]

"Hi!" is three bytes → six hex digits; "café" is five bytes → 636166c3a9.

Example 2: Control Bytes¶

const pluss::Note n = pluss::make_note("\n\t").hex_encode();
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"0a09"

Newline (0a) and tab (09).

Example 3: Round-Trips Through hex_decode¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({"payload", "€"}).hex_encode().hex_decode())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["payload", "€"]
